resources.string: Mouth in sagittal section
From chewing to an oral bolus
Hard palate
The hard palate forms a firm roof against which the tongue can press food.
Tongue surface
The tongue collects wetted particles and shapes them into a bolus.
Oropharyngeal opening
The tongue moves a prepared bolus toward the shared passage behind the mouth.
Teeth break food into smaller pieces.
Saliva moistens the particles and begins some starch digestion.
Against the palate, the tongue gathers food into a bolus.
The tongue propels the bolus toward the oropharynx.
Molar in longitudinal section
How a molar withstands chewing
Enamel
A highly mineralized outer layer covers the crown, not the root.
Dentin
Dentin forms much of the tooth beneath the enamel and around the pulp.
Pulp and root canal
Soft pulp contains vessels and nerves. Root canals connect the pulp to nearby tissue.
Root support
Periodontal tissues anchor the root to the surrounding alveolar bone.
The crown contacts and crushes food.
Enamel and dentin distribute chewing load.
Periodontal tissues support the roots as force reaches the jaw.
Vessels and nerves within the pulp supply and sense the tooth.
Esophageal wall and lumen
A bolus traveling down the esophagus
Upper inlet
The upper esophageal sphincter relaxes briefly to admit a swallowed bolus.
Circular muscle
Behind the bolus, a coordinated circular contraction narrows the lumen.
Distal lumen
A peristaltic wave moves the bolus downward; transport is not simply gravity.
Gastroesophageal junction
The lower sphincter region relaxes for passage into the stomach and subsequently restores tone.
Swallowing allows the bolus to pass through the upper inlet.
A coordinated contraction forms behind the bolus.
Esophageal peristalsis moves the bolus toward the stomach.
The bolus passes through the lower sphincter region.
Stomach cutaway
Storage, mixing and release in the stomach
Fundus
The proximal stomach accommodates incoming food without acting as a rigid container.
Rugae
These mucosal folds flatten as the stomach expands.
Antrum
Contractions here mix and grind contents; much can be pushed back into the stomach.
Pylorus
The outlet meters the passage of chyme into the duodenum.
The proximal stomach receives and stores food.
Gastric secretions mix with the contents and start protein digestion.
Antral contractions grind the contents and can push them backward.
Small amounts of chyme pass through the pylorus.
Regional map of the small intestine
Digestion and absorption along the small intestine
Duodenal region
Chyme meets bile and pancreatic secretions just after leaving the stomach.
Jejunal region
Folds and villi give a large interface for absorption of digested nutrients.
Terminal region
The distal ileum carries out specialized absorption before reaching the large intestine.
The duodenum receives chyme and digestive secretions.
Mixing brings digested nutrients near the intestinal surface.
Nutrients cross the epithelium toward blood or lymph.
Remaining contents pass from the terminal ileum to the cecum.
Duodenal loop and duct openings
Neutralization and mixing in the duodenum
Duodenal bulb
The first segment receives acidic chyme through the pylorus.
Major papilla
Bile and pancreatic secretions commonly enter at this opening; duct anatomy can vary.
Distal loop
Contents turn toward the jejunum after mixing.
Acidic chyme enters the first portion.
Bicarbonate in pancreatic fluid helps neutralize acid.
Bile and digestive enzymes mix with chyme.
The mixture moves onward to the jejunum.
Jejunal fold and villi
From the jejunal lumen to blood and lymph
Circular fold
A fold of mucosa and submucosa increases the area exposed to luminal contents.
Villus epithelium
Absorptive cells line the villus. Their much smaller microvilli are not drawn here.
Villus capillaries
Soluble nutrients such as absorbed monosaccharides are carried away by blood.
Central lacteal
Many long-chain dietary lipids initially leave the villus in lymph after processing by enterocytes.
Mixing brings nutrients to the folded mucosal surface.
Transport across the villus epithelium moves nutrients out of the lumen.
Many water-soluble nutrients enter the blood capillaries.
Lymph carries many of the processed long-chain lipids.
Terminal ileum and ileocecal junction
Specialized uptake in the terminal ileum
Ileal wall
The terminal ileum has absorptive epithelium and specialized transport mechanisms.
Lymphoid patches
Aggregated lymphoid follicles are prominent in the ileum, distinct from absorptive villi.
Ileocecal junction
The junction regulates movement into the cecum and helps limit backflow.
Digested contents reach the distal small intestine.
The terminal ileum reclaims bile salts and absorbs vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor.
Local lymphoid patches participate in mucosal monitoring.
Remaining contents pass through the ileocecal junction.
Large intestine from the front
Water recovery and transport through the large intestine
Cecal inlet
This is where ileal contents first enter the large intestine.
Transverse colon
The colon absorbs water and electrolytes and transports residual contents.
Sigmoid turn
The left colon continues into the sigmoid segment before reaching the rectum.
Rectal region
The rectum can hold stool before defecation.
Residual contents enter the cecum from the ileum.
Water and electrolytes continue to be absorbed as contents pass.
Intermittent contractions propel contents toward the rectum.
The rectum temporarily holds stool until evacuation.
Cecum, ileal opening and appendix origin
Entry of ileal contents into the cecum
Ileal opening
The terminal ileum joins the cecum on its medial side.
Blind pouch
The cecum extends below the ileal opening, forming a pouch.
Appendiceal origin
The appendix arises from the cecum; this is not the route onward through the colon.
Ileal contents cross the ileocecal junction.
Contents enter the cecal pouch and mix locally.
The pouch has a separate narrow opening to the appendix.
The main stream continues into the ascending colon.
Appendix wall in cross-section
Local immune monitoring in the appendix
Appendiceal lumen
The narrow lumen communicates with the cecum but terminates blindly.
Mucosal lining
The mucosa interfaces with material present in the appendiceal lumen.
Lymphoid follicle
Lymphoid follicles in the wall are part of the gut mucosal immune system.
Material can reach the appendix from the cecum.
It encounters the mucosal lining.
Immune cells in the wall survey material near the lining.
Local lymphoid signaling can support mucosal responses.
Colon segment and mucosal crypts
Water recovery at the colon wall
Haustral contour
The sacculated outer contour is a gross feature, not a microscopic villus.
Crypts
The colonic surface has crypt openings, not small-intestinal villi.
Absorptive surface
Surface epithelial cells absorb water and electrolytes while mucus helps contents move.
Contents pause and mix during local contractions.
The lumen contacts a mucosal surface with crypts.
Water and electrolytes are recovered across the epithelium.
Propulsive contractions move the remaining material onward.
Rectum and pelvic floor
Rectal filling and the urge to defecate
Rectal inlet
Material arrives from the sigmoid colon.
Rectal ampulla
The expandable region can store stool temporarily.
Pelvic floor sling
Puborectalis helps maintain the anorectal angle at rest.
Stool arrives from the sigmoid colon.
Filling stretches the rectal wall.
Stretch contributes to an urge and reflex relaxation of the internal sphincter.
Pelvic floor and external sphincter coordination affects whether evacuation follows.
Anal canal and sphincter layers
Continence and coordinated opening
Internal sphincter
The inner smooth muscle maintains involuntary tone and responds to rectal filling.
External sphincter
The outer skeletal muscle can contract under voluntary control.
Epithelial transition
The canal lining changes as it approaches the exterior; boundary detail is simplified.
At rest, sphincter tone and the pelvic floor help maintain continence.
Rectal filling can briefly relax the internal sphincter.
External sphincter contraction can defer evacuation.
During evacuation, coordinated relaxation allows passage through the canal.
One representative path, not the speed, timing, or amount of digestion or transport.
The highlighted region explains the current step; no time or rate is measured.
The small-intestinal map is unfolded and not to scale.
Front view: the person\'s right side is on the left of the screen.
The appendix opening is a landmark, not the main route through the cecum.
Ideal villus surface area
Equal, non-overlapping cylindrical villi on a flat 1 mm² patch. Excludes folds, microvilli and transport. Not an estimate of personal absorption.
Area ratio = 1 + density × 2π × radius × height. The tip area replaces the same area at the base.
